system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2171-03-28 17:02:00 to 2171-03-31 16:05:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for left upper quadrant abdominal pain near her gastrostomy tube site. She has a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and cyclic vomiting syndrome requiring a gastrostomy tube for nutritional support. She underwent fluoroscopy-guided replacement of the gastrostomy tube due to malposition and granulation tissue at the site, which was treated with silver nitrate. Post-procedure, her pain improved, and she tolerated oral intake. The decision was made not to restart tube feeds due to anatomical concerns. She was restarted on home medications with an increase in nortriptyline to 100 mg nightly for pain management and discharged home with instructions for tube site care, pain control, and follow-up endoscopy.

Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the Bariatric Surgery Service at ___ 
___ after undergoing a G-tube 
removal.
 
Please call your surgeon or return to the emergency department 
if you develop a fever greater than 101.5, chest pain, shortness 
of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain unrelieved by your pain 
medication, severe nausea or vomiting, severe abdominal 
bloating, inability to eat or drink, foul smelling or colorful 
drainage from your incisions, redness or swelling around your 
incisions, or any other symptoms which are concerning to you.
 
Diet: Stay on Stage IV diet until your follow up appointment. Do 
not self advance diet, do not drink out of a straw or chew gum. 
Please also eat small snacks right when you wake up, between 
meals, and right before bedtime.  Please check your blood sugar 
right when you wake up, 2 hours after each meal, before bed, 
when you feel symptoms of low blood suger (nausea, sweating, 
lightheadedness), and anytime you have been fasting for 4 hours 
or longer during the day. If your blood sugar is below 70, 
please eat a small snack and check your blood sugar again 15 
minutes later.

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are not being discharged with medication for pain. You 
may take liquid tylenol for pain if you experience any in the 
coming days, although it is not expected that you will.
2. You should begin taking a chewable complete multivitamin with 
minerals. No gummy vitamins.
3. You should take a stool softener, Colace, twice daily for 
constipation as needed, or until you resume a normal bowel 
pattern.
4. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

Activity:
No heavy lifting of items ___ pounds for 6 weeks. You may 
resume moderate exercise at your discretion, no abdominal 
exercises.

Wound Care:
You may shower, no tub baths or swimming.
If there is clear drainage from your incisions, cover with 
clean, dry gauze.
Your steri-strips will fall off on their own. Please remove any 
remaining strips ___ days after surgery.
Please call the doctor if you have increased pain, swelling, 
redness, or drainage from the incision sites.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I just had my gastrostomy tube removed today at the clinic, and since then I’ve been feeling really shaky, dizzy, and I had tingling in my fingers and lips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you eat anything before the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t eat all day. I was nervous about the visit, and I’ve been stressed from a trip I just got back from. I also had diarrhea during the car ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When we checked your blood sugar at the clinic, it was very low—only 35. That explains the dizziness and tingling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is that because I didn’t eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, yes. But because of your gastric bypass surgery, your body processes food and sugar differently. Skipping meals can cause your blood sugar to drop quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it could get that low. After they gave me apple juice, I felt better, but then I had cramping and diarrhea again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called ‘dumping syndrome.’ When sugar enters your intestine too fast, it can cause cramps, nausea, and diarrhea. We’ll help you avoid that going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. So why am I being admitted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your blood sugar dropped so low and you’ve been having trouble eating, we want to monitor you closely and make sure you’re stable before going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I do feel better now, but I’m still a little shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on IV fluids with some sugar to help stabilize your levels. We’ll also check your blood sugar regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Should I be worried about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a plan to prevent it. You’ll need to eat small, frequent snacks—even when you’re not hungry—especially first thing in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my diet? I was on a bariatric diet before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on Stage 1—clear liquids—and slowly advance as you tolerate it. By tomorrow, if all goes well, we’ll move you up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. I had some broth last night and didn’t feel sick. But I’ve been burping a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after surgery and with the changes in your digestion. It should improve as you start eating more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My blood sugar was 88 this morning when the nurse checked it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great improvement. We’ll keep monitoring it. We also did an X-ray this morning to make sure everything looks okay in your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small amount of contrast left from your procedure, but no signs of a blockage or free air. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Can I move up to a thicker diet today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll advance you to Stage 2 today—full liquids like yogurt and pudding. We’ll keep an eye on how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re doing well. Blood sugars are stable, and you’ve been tolerating your diet. We’re going to move you to Stage 4 today—soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I’m actually feeling hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Just remember to eat slowly and in small amounts. We also want to talk about your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking my nortriptyline and quetiapine. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those. We’re also adding pantoprazole twice a day to protect your stomach, since you’ve had ulcers in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and what about pain? I’ve had some mild discomfort at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave IV pain medication yesterday, but now you can take liquid Tylenol if needed. The pain should continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And no ibuprofen, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers. Stick to Tylenol only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, eating well, and your blood sugar is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the Stage 4 diet, eat small snacks throughout the day, and check your blood sugar regularly—especially if you feel shaky or dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my blood sugar is low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eat a small snack with some carbs, wait 15 minutes, and check again. We’ve also prescribed promethazine for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and when should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have a fever, severe pain, redness or drainage from the site, or can’t keep food down. Otherwise, follow up with your surgeon in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be able to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. Ate a soft meal and my blood sugar was 92 an hour ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to crush all your pills so they’re easier to absorb, and start taking the chewable multivitamin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And no heavy lifting for six weeks, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. You can walk and do light activity, but avoid anything strenuous, especially involving your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted following gastrostomy tube removal due to symptomatic hypoglycemia with blood glucose of 35 mg/dL, likely exacerbated by fasting and her history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She experienced dumping syndrome after oral glucose administration and required IV dextrose and close metabolic monitoring. During her hospitalization, she was advanced from clear liquids to a Stage IV bariatric diet without complications, remained hemodynamically stable, and had no further episodes of hypoglycemia. She was discharged home with instructions on frequent small meals, blood glucose monitoring, wound care, and medication management, including new prescriptions for pantoprazole and promethazine. Follow-up was arranged to monitor for long-term metabolic and gastrointestinal stability.
